le:job-loss:coverage.plain: When job-based health coverage ends, two clocks start. COBRA lets you stay on the same employer plan, generally for up to 18 months after a job loss. You get at least 60 days to sign up. If you sign up in that time, coverage reaches back to the day your job coverage ended, and you pay the premiums for that time. It can cost up to 102% of the full premium, because your employer stops paying its share. Losing coverage also lets you sign up on the Marketplace within 60 days. There, help with premiums is based on what you expect to earn this year, which may now be less. Count severance, unemployment pay, any 401(k) money you take out and pay from a new job. Tell the Marketplace about income changes right away. Starting with 2026, if you got more help than you qualify for, you must pay all of it back at tax time, and household income above 400% of the poverty line generally gets no federal help. Medicaid, and CHIP for children, take applications any time of year and look at what you earn each month now. If your spouse has a job-based plan, it must give you at least 30 days to join. If you choose COBRA and later drop it or stop paying, the Marketplace does not open again for you: once 60 days have passed since your job coverage ended, you usually have to wait for open enrollment, unless COBRA runs out, your old employer stops paying part of it, or you have another life event. Compare every option by total cost, not just the monthly premium.
props: Losing job-based coverage starts two time windows
COBRA keeps the same employer plan, generally up to 18 months after job loss
COBRA election window is at least 60 days
at least 60 days to sign up
An election made within the window covers you back to when job coverage ended, and the premiums for that time are owed
coverage reaches back to the day
COBRA premium can be up to 102% of full cost
Loss of coverage triggers a 60-day Marketplace special enrollment period
Premium tax credits are based on expected income for the year, which may be lower
what you expect to earn this year
Count severance, unemployment pay, any 401(k) withdrawal and new-job wages in the income estimate
Report income changes to the Marketplace as they happen
tell the marketplace about income changes right away
Starting with 2026, excess advance credits must be repaid in full
pay all of it back at tax time
Household income above 400% of the poverty line generally gets no credit
Medicaid and CHIP accept applications any time of year and judge eligibility on current monthly income
take applications any time of year
A spouse's employer plan must offer at least 30 days to enroll

Dropping COBRA or stopping payment does not reopen the Marketplace; once 60 days have passed since job coverage ended, generally wait for open enrollment unless COBRA runs out, an employer subsidy ends, or another life event occurs
usually have to wait for open enrollment
Compare all options on total cost, not premium alone

le:job-loss:runway.plain: Divide your cash savings by what you must spend each month. That is how many months you can last. Unemployment pay is run by your state, so apply with your state soon. It counts as income for federal tax, so think about having tax taken out. Severance is taxed like pay and usually has tax taken out already. If money is tight, pay for housing, utilities, food, insurance, the transportation that gets you to work and any payments a court has ordered, such as child support, first. Then keep at least the minimum payment on every debt current, and call your lenders about hardship plans before you miss a payment. For federal student loans, ask your loan servicer about an income-driven plan, where the payment can be as low as $0 in some cases, or an unemployment deferment. Keep paying until a deferment is approved.
props: Runway = liquid savings / essential monthly spending
divide your cash savings by what you must spend each month
Unemployment insurance is state-run; file promptly with the state
UI benefits are federally taxable; consider voluntary withholding
Severance is taxable wages, normally withheld
When cash is tight, essentials and court-ordered payments (such as child support) first, then minimum payments on every debt kept current
Hardship plans: call lenders before a payment is missed
Federal student loans: ask about an income-driven plan (payment can be as low as $0) or an unemployment deferment
Keep paying until a deferment is granted
keep paying until a deferment is approved

le:job-loss:old-401k.plain: For the old job's retirement plan, the usual choices are: leave it in the old plan, move it to your new job's plan, or move it to an IRA. Cashing it out means income tax, plus an extra 10% tax before age 59½ unless an exception applies. A check made out to you also has 20% held back for tax. Moving the money straight from one account to the other (a direct rollover) avoids both. If you left the job in or after the year you turn 55, that plan — not an IRA — can pay you without the extra 10% tax. That is a reason to leave it where it is if you might need it. If the plan holds your employer's stock, look into net unrealized appreciation before moving it, because putting those shares into an IRA loses that tax treatment. If you still owe on a 401(k) loan, find out when it comes due: an unpaid balance counts as a withdrawal (taxed, plus the extra 10% tax before 59½), but if the plan takes the loan out of your balance within 12 months after you leave, you can still roll that amount over until your tax-filing deadline, including extensions, for that year.
props: Options: leave, roll to new plan, roll to IRA
leave it in the old plan
Cash-out triggers income tax plus 10% additional tax before 59½ absent an exception
A check paid to you carries 20% mandatory withholding
A direct trustee-to-trustee rollover avoids both
Separation in/after the year you turn 55: that plan (not an IRA) pays without the 10% tax
This argues for leaving it in place if you may need it
Check NUA before rolling employer stock; rolling shares to an IRA forfeits it
An unpaid 401(k) loan balance is treated as a taxable distribution (plus 10% before 59½)
A plan-loan offset within 12 months after leaving can be rolled over until the tax-filing deadline (with extensions)
The offset must occur within 12 months after leaving the job

le:job-loss:equity.plain: Stock options that have vested often expire a set time after you leave. Incentive stock options lose their special tax treatment if you don't exercise them within three months after your job ends. Your grant agreement has the exact deadline — read it before it passes.
props: Vested options often expire a fixed period after leaving
expire a set time after you leave
ISOs lose favorable treatment if not exercised within three months of termination
The exact window is in the grant agreement; read it before it closes

le:job-loss:withholding.plain: A year with a gap, severance and two employers often ends with too much or too little tax taken out. Use the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator and give your new employer a new Form W-4. Each employer's payroll only tracks its own 401(k). But the yearly limit on what you put in ({{fig:limit_401k_deferral}} for 2026) is yours across all plans, so add up both jobs' contributions yourself.
props: Gap + severance + two employers is the classic mis-withholding year
too much or too little tax
Run the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator and file a new W-4
Each employer's payroll tracks the limit separately
The employee deferral limit (2026 figure) applies across all plans; total both yourself

le:new-baby:enroll.plain: A birth or adoption gives you a special window to add your child to health coverage: at least 30 days for a job-based plan and 60 days on the Marketplace. Miss it and you may have to wait for the next open enrollment.
props: At least 30 days for employer group plans
Missing it can mean waiting for the next open enrollment

le:new-baby:ssn.plain: To claim the Child Tax Credit (up to {{fig:ctc_per_child}} per child), your child needs a Social Security number. You can usually ask for one at the hospital when you register the birth.
props: The child's SSN is needed to claim the CTC
It is usually requested at the hospital with birth registration
The credit is up to the figures-layer amount per child

le:new-baby:protection.plain: A child who depends on you is the main reason to have term life insurance. A common rule of thumb is 10–12 times the main earner's income; the DIME method gives a number that fits your household. A will is where you name a guardian for a young child — without one, a court chooses. Update the beneficiaries on your accounts at the same time. Don't name a young child as a beneficiary directly: a court may have to appoint someone to hold the money. Name a trust, or a custodian under your state's law for gifts to minors, instead.
props: A dependent is the main reason to own term life
main reason to have term life
DIME gives a more specific number
A will names a guardian for a minor child; without one a court decides
Update beneficiary designations at the same time
Do not name a minor directly: the money can end up with a court-appointed guardian
a court may have to appoint someone
Name a trust or a custodian under the state's transfers-to-minors act instead

le:new-baby:childcare.plain: A dependent-care FSA lets you pay for childcare with money that skips income and payroll tax (2026 limit: {{fig:limit_dcfsa}} per household, {{fig:limit_dcfsa_mfs}} if married filing separately). Costs you pay through the FSA can't also count toward the child and dependent care credit. So plan the two together instead of trying to max both.
props: A DCFSA shelters childcare costs from income and payroll tax
FSA-reimbursed expenses cannot also count for the credit
The two must be coordinated, not both maxed
The 2026 limit is per household, with a lower amount for married filing separately

le:new-baby:529.plain: A 529 plan grows tax-free when used for school costs, and about 30 states give a state tax deduction for putting money in. This tool puts education saving after your own retirement accounts, because a student can borrow for college but a retiree can't borrow for retirement.
props: 529s grow tax-free for qualified education costs
About 30 states offer a state income tax deduction
The framework sequences education after tax-advantaged retirement steps
because students can borrow, retirees cannot (mechanism)

le:marriage:enroll.plain: Getting married opens a special window to change health plans: at least 30 days for job-based plans and 60 days on the Marketplace. Compare both employers' plans by premium plus the costs you expect to pay yourself, including any extra charge for covering a spouse.
props: At least 30 days employer / 60 days Marketplace
Compare on premium plus expected out-of-pocket, incl. spousal surcharge
extra charge for covering a spouse

le:marriage:names.plain: If either of you changes your name, update it with Social Security before you file taxes. If your tax return and Social Security's records don't match, your return can be delayed.
props: Update the name with SSA before filing
A mismatch with SSA records can delay processing

le:marriage:filing.plain: Whether you count as married for taxes depends on December 31. So a December wedding counts for the whole year. Two paychecks each taxed as if single often don't have enough tax taken out once you're combined. Use the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator together and file new W-4s.
props: Filing status is set by marital status on December 31
A December wedding counts for the whole year
Two incomes withheld as single often under-withhold combined
don't have enough tax taken out
Run the estimator together and file new W-4s

le:marriage:beneficiaries.plain: Retirement accounts and life insurance go to whoever is named on the beneficiary form, not to whoever is named in a will. In a 401(k), federal law generally makes your spouse the default beneficiary unless they give that up in writing. IRAs go to whoever the form names. Read every form instead of assuming.
props: Retirement accounts and life insurance pass by beneficiary form, not will
not to whoever is named in a will
401(k): spouse is generally default beneficiary unless they waive in writing
iras go to whoever the form names

le:marriage:align.plain: Take the diagnostic together. Its questions about whether you agree exist because couples who disagree on risk or goals tend to get stuck on every other step. Export the plan as Markdown so you both work from the same list.
props: Spousal-alignment questions exist because disagreeing couples stall
Export as Markdown to share one list

le:divorce:counsel.plain: Divorce is the one event on this list where a lawyer is close to a must: your state's property law decides what counts as shared, and a signed agreement is hard to undo. If you can't pay a lawyer for the whole case, look for legal aid or ask whether a lawyer will help with just part of it. First, list every account, debt and insurance policy. That list is also the start of your own net-worth snapshot. The divorce papers don't bind your lenders: until a shared debt is paid off, refinanced without your name, or the lender lets you off it, the lender can usually still make you pay.
props: Professional counsel is close to mandatory for divorce
State property law decides what is marital
If a full-service lawyer is unaffordable, look for legal aid or ask about a lawyer for only part of the case
Build a complete inventory of accounts, debts, policies first
list every account, debt and insurance policy
The inventory starts your own net-worth snapshot
A decree does not bind lenders; a creditor can generally collect on a joint debt until it is paid off, refinanced without your name, or you are released

le:divorce:qdro.plain: A job-based plan can only pay a former spouse under a court order called a qualified domestic relations order (QDRO). Money paid to the former spouse under a QDRO skips the extra 10% tax, but that break does not apply to withdrawals from an IRA, so it is lost if the money is moved into an IRA first. An IRA is split by a transfer made as part of the divorce, which isn't taxed as a withdrawal. Cashing out instead of using these routes can turn the split into a tax bill. Compare what each share is worth after tax: pre-tax retirement money is taxed when you take it out, qualified Roth withdrawals are not, and stock you receive keeps your spouse's old tax cost, so a dollar of each is not worth the same.
props: Employer plans pay a former spouse only under a QDRO
QDRO distributions to the alternate payee are exempt from the 10% additional tax
The exemption does not apply to IRA withdrawals, so rolling the money into an IRA first loses it
IRAs are divided by transfer incident to divorce, not taxable
transfer made as part of the divorce
Cashing out instead can create a tax bill
Compare shares after tax: pre-tax money is taxed on withdrawal, qualified Roth withdrawals are not, received stock keeps the old basis

le:divorce:beneficiaries.plain: Many states automatically remove an ex-spouse as beneficiary on some accounts. But for job-based plans covered by ERISA, the Supreme Court ruled that the plan's own papers win (Egelhoff v. Egelhoff, 2001). Don't count on state law: file new beneficiary forms on every account and policy.
props: Many states auto-revoke an ex-spouse on some non-probate assets
For ERISA plans, plan documents control (Egelhoff, 2001)
File new forms everywhere rather than relying on state law

le:divorce:filing.plain: Whether you're married on December 31 sets your filing status for the year. Losing coverage under a spouse's plan lets you use COBRA (up to 36 months for a former spouse) and opens a Marketplace special enrollment window. For a divorce or legal separation, the law puts the notice on you or your former spouse: tell the plan administrator within 60 days of the event, or you can lose the COBRA right.
props: Marital status on Dec 31 sets filing status
Losing spouse-plan coverage is a COBRA qualifying event, up to 36 months for a former spouse
It is also a Marketplace special enrollment trigger
After divorce or legal separation, the employee or former spouse must notify the plan within 60 days or the COBRA right can be lost

le:divorce:rebuild.plain: A home that ran on two incomes now runs on one. That usually means a bigger emergency fund target, and taking the diagnostic again with your new answers.
props: Usually means a larger emergency-fund target

le:home-purchase:afford.plain: Your down payment is a short-term goal kept in safe places. Your emergency fund is separate money, and it should still be full after closing — as an owner, you now pay for repairs a landlord used to cover.
props: The down payment is a near-term goal in safe assets
The emergency fund is a separate pool, whole after closing
repairs a landlord used to cover

le:home-purchase:insure.plain: Lenders require homeowners insurance. A standard homeowners policy does not cover flood damage. Flood insurance is a separate policy (from NFIP or a private insurer), and there is usually a waiting period before it starts.
props: Flood is a separate NFIP or private policy
Usually a waiting period before it takes effect

le:home-purchase:pmi.plain: With a conventional loan, the lender must drop private mortgage insurance on its own once your balance is scheduled to reach 78% of the home's original value and you are up to date on payments. You can ask for it to be removed at 80%. Write down the date. FHA loans follow HUD's rules instead. On FHA loans started after mid-2013, if you borrowed more than 90% of the home's value, the yearly premium lasts for the whole loan (up to 30 years). If you borrowed 90% or less, it lasts up to 11 years. Your Closing Disclosure shows which loan type you have.
props: PMI terminates automatically at scheduled 78% of original value (conventional loans)
Automatic termination happens once you are current on payments
FHA mortgage insurance follows HUD's rules, not these
Scope: FHA loans started after mid-2013
Borrowed more than 90%: annual premium lasts the whole loan term, up to 30 years
The Closing Disclosure names the loan type
shows which loan type you have

le:home-purchase:umbrella.plain: Owning a home raises what you could lose if someone sues you. An umbrella policy adds coverage on top of your home and auto liability, and it costs little for the amount of coverage you get.
props: Owning a home raises lawsuit exposure
Umbrella sits on top of homeowners and auto liability
on top of your home and auto liability
It is inexpensive per dollar of coverage

le:home-purchase:sale-later.plain: When you sell your main home, you can leave out up to {{fig:sec121_exclusion_single}} ({{fig:sec121_exclusion_mfj}} on a qualifying joint return) of profit from tax if you owned it and lived in it for two of the five years before selling. Money spent on improvements raises your cost basis, so keep the receipts.
props: Gain on a main home can be excluded up to the §121 amount
Requires owning and living there 2 of the 5 years before sale
Capital improvements add to basis; keep receipts
A qualifying joint return gets the higher exclusion amount

le:relocation:residency.plain: Each state decides for itself who counts as a resident. The year you move, you usually file a part-year resident return in each state. If you're leaving a high-tax state, you often have to prove you left, so keep proof of the move — a lease or deed, driver's license, voter registration.
props: A move year usually means part-year returns in each state
Leaving a high-tax state, the burden of proof often falls on you
Keep evidence: lease/deed, license, voter registration

le:relocation:coverage.plain: A permanent move to an area where your plan isn't offered lets you sign up for a new Marketplace plan within 60 days. Job-based plans may have a different network of doctors in the new state.
props: A permanent move out of the plan's area triggers a 60-day Marketplace SEP
Employer plans may have different networks in the new state

le:relocation:insurance.plain: Each state sets its own auto insurance rules and prices, so your policy must be rewritten for the new state. Make sure your liability limits still fit what you own, not just the new state's minimum.
props: Auto requirements and prices are state-by-state; policy must be rewritten
Liability limits should match assets, not the state minimum
not just the new state's minimum

le:relocation:expenses.plain: Most people can't deduct moving costs on their federal taxes (active-duty military moving under orders still can, and from 2026 so can intelligence-community employees who relocate for a new assignment). For everyone else, if your employer pays for your move, that counts as taxable pay.
props: The federal moving-expense deduction is unavailable to most taxpayers
For everyone else, employer-paid moving costs are taxable wages
Exception from 2026: intelligence-community employees relocating on assignment

le:relocation:estate.plain: Wills, powers of attorney and healthcare directives follow state law. Papers that were valid where you signed them usually still count, but having them reviewed in your new state catches differences in signing rules and in how agents are named.
props: Estate documents are governed by state law
Documents valid where signed are usually honored
A review in the new state catches execution and agent-designation differences

le:windfall:park.plain: Financial planners often suggest waiting a few months — with the money in an insured savings account or Treasury bills — before making big decisions. The point is about behavior: sudden money invites rushed purchases and pressure from other people. Deposit insurance covers {{fig:fdic_standard_max_deposit}} for each depositor at each bank, for each type of account ownership, so split a larger amount across banks or buy Treasury bills. Three things can't wait for that pause. If anyone in your household gets SSI, Medicaid, SNAP or housing help, a lump sum can end that help (SSI's limit on what you can own is {{fig:ssi_resource_limit_individual}} for one person), so report it and ask before you move the money; an ABLE account or a special-needs trust can sometimes keep a person with a disability eligible. Windfalls that are taxable — lottery or gambling wins, back pay, most legal settlements that are not for a physical injury or sickness — count as income for the year, so set the tax money aside; if not enough tax was withheld, paying estimated tax can help you avoid a penalty. And if you inherited the money and might turn it down (a "disclaimer"), you generally must do that in writing within 9 months and before you accept it; using the money or telling others what to do with it can count as accepting.
props: Planners commonly advise a cooling-off period
often suggest waiting a few months
Park in insured savings or T-bills
Purpose is behavioral: rushed purchases and pressure from others
Deposit insurance limit per depositor, per bank, per ownership category
Spread a larger sum across banks or hold T-bills
split a larger amount across banks
A windfall can end SSI, Medicaid, SNAP or housing help; SSI resource limit for an individual; report and ask
An ABLE account or special-needs trust can sometimes preserve eligibility for a person with a disability
Taxable windfalls (lottery, gambling, back pay, non-physical-injury settlements) are income; set tax aside
If withholding is short, an estimated payment can help avoid an underpayment penalty
A disclaimer must generally be written, within 9 months, before acceptance
Using the asset or directing what happens to it can count as acceptance

le:windfall:character.plain: Cash, a brokerage account, an inherited IRA and a house are taxed in different ways. Inherited things usually get a new cost basis equal to their value on the day of death (a "step-up"), so selling soon after you inherit often creates little taxable gain. Most people who inherit an IRA from someone other than a spouse must empty it within 10 years. If the original owner had already started required withdrawals, you must also take yearly withdrawals during those years. If you inherit an IRA from someone other than a spouse, you can't roll it into your own IRA. Move it only by a direct transfer from one company to the other, into an account labeled as inherited; a check made out to you counts as a withdrawal and can't be put back.
props: Different asset types are taxed differently
Inherited assets generally get basis stepped up to date-of-death value
So selling soon after inheriting often produces little gain
Most non-spouse IRA beneficiaries must empty it within 10 years
If the owner had begun RMDs, annual distributions are required too
A non-spouse beneficiary cannot roll an inherited IRA into their own
can't roll it into your own ira
Move it only by trustee-to-trustee transfer into an inherited-titled account
A check paid to the beneficiary counts as a withdrawal and cannot be put back

le:windfall:sequence.plain: A windfall doesn't need a new plan — it speeds up the one you have. Pay off high-interest debt, finish the emergency fund, then fill tax-advantaged accounts before investing in a regular taxable account.
props: A windfall accelerates the existing plan rather than needing a new one
speeds up the one you have
Order: high-interest debt, emergency fund, tax-advantaged space, then taxable

le:windfall:lump-sum.plain: Vanguard looked at past market history and found that investing a lump sum right away beat spreading it out over time in about two-thirds of the periods it studied, because markets go up more often than they go down. Spreading it out protects you from regret if the market falls right after you invest. Both are reasonable; choose the one you'll stick with.
props: Vanguard's historical study: lump sum beat DCA in about two-thirds of rolling periods
because markets rise more often than fall (mechanism)
DCA buys protection against regret after an early drop
Both defensible; pick the one you will stick with

le:windfall:gift.plain: If you give someone more than the yearly exclusion ({{fig:gift_annual_exclusion}} per person for 2026), you have to file a gift-tax return, but you rarely owe tax, because it counts against your lifetime exemption ({{fig:estate_exemption_individual}} per person for 2026).
props: Gifts above the annual exclusion require a gift-tax return
Rarely any tax, because they count against the lifetime exemption

le:retirement:medicare.plain: Your first chance to sign up for Medicare lasts seven months around your 65th birthday: three months before, your birthday month, and three months after. If you sign up late for Part B and had no other qualifying coverage, you pay a higher premium for life. COBRA or retiree coverage does not count: generally only coverage from your own or your spouse's current job lets you delay Part B without that penalty. If you keep putting money in an HSA after 65, stop six months before you apply for Medicare or Social Security, because Part A can start up to six months back. Your retirement income also sets extra Medicare charges (IRMAA), based on your income from two years earlier.
props: Initial enrollment period is seven months around the 65th birthday
Three before, the birthday month, three after
Late Part B without other qualifying coverage → lifetime premium penalty
COBRA and retiree coverage do not count; generally only current-employment coverage allows delaying Part B
If contributing to an HSA after 65, stop six months before applying for Medicare or Social Security
Part A coverage reaches back up to six months
Retirement income drives IRMAA with a two-year lookback

le:retirement:social-security.plain: Whether you claim at 62, at full retirement age, or at 70 is one of the biggest money choices most retirees make. For a married person who earned more, waiting also raises what the surviving spouse would get.
props: Claiming at 62 / FRA / 70 is among the largest retiree decisions
one of the biggest money choices
For a married higher earner, delay also raises the survivor benefit

le:retirement:withdrawals.plain: Which accounts you take money from first, and how much you take, shapes the taxes you pay over your life and how exposed you are to a bad run of early market returns.
props: Withdrawal order and rate set lifetime tax
taxes you pay over your life
bad run of early market returns

le:retirement:rmd.plain: Required minimum distributions from traditional accounts start at age 73, or at age 75 if you were born in 1960 or later. You can wait until April 1 of the next year for the first one, but then you take two in the same tax year. If you still work, you can usually wait on your current employer's plan until you retire. Giving straight from an IRA to charity (a qualified charitable distribution, allowed from age 70½) can count toward them without adding to your income.
props: age 75 if you were born in 1960
First RMD can wait until April 1 of the next year
…at the cost of two RMDs in one tax year
two in the same tax year
Current employer's plan can usually wait until retirement
QCDs from age 70½ can satisfy RMDs without adding to income

le:retirement:ltc.plain: About 70% of Americans turning 65 will need some long-term care. More people get this care at home than in a facility, and much of it is unpaid help. Medicare and Medigap do not pay for this kind of care. Medicaid does if you meet your state's rules on income, savings and how much care you need. Otherwise the choice is between buying insurance, paying for it yourself, or a mix. For long-term care insurance, the premium can go up after you buy.
props: About 70% of those turning 65 will need some LTC
More people get care at home than in facilities
at home than in a facility
Medicare and Medigap do not pay for long-term care
do not pay for this kind of care
Medicaid pays if you meet the state's income, asset and care-need rules

le:death-of-spouse:pause.plain: A few clocks start now, and the rest can wait. If your health insurance came through your spouse's job, the COBRA and Marketplace windows start when that coverage ends (you have 60 days to act), and if you want to turn down an inheritance you generally must do it within 9 months and before you accept it. Ask a tax preparer or estate lawyer whether to file an estate tax return for your spouse (usually due in 9 months). It can pass your spouse's unused exemption to you even when no tax is owed. If a debt collector asks you to pay your spouse's debts, don't use your own money until you check. The estate usually pays them. You usually owe only debts that were joint or that you co-signed (being an authorized user on a card is not joint), or debts your state's law makes a surviving spouse pay. Selling the house, moving, or taking a lump sum can wait. Find the will, insurance policies and account statements, and get several certified copies of the death certificate — most companies will ask for one.
props: A few deadlines start now; the rest can wait
Irreversible moves (sell house, move, lump sum) can wait
Get several certified death certificates; most institutions ask for one
COBRA and Marketplace windows start at loss of spouse-employer coverage; 60 days
A disclaimer must generally be made within 9 months and before accepting the asset
Ask whether to file an estate-tax return for the spouse (generally due in 9 months); it can pass the unused exemption even when no tax is owed
If a collector asks you to pay the spouse's debts, do not use your own money until you have checked
The estate generally pays the debts; you usually owe only joint or co-signed debts (an authorized user is not joint) or ones state law puts on a surviving spouse

le:death-of-spouse:notify.plain: Tell the Social Security Administration about the death (the funeral home often does this). A surviving spouse can get survivor benefits as early as age 60 (50 if disabled), and at any age if they have not remarried and are caring for the deceased's child who is under 16 or disabled and qualifies for child's benefits. The children can get benefits of their own while under 18 (19 if still in high school), and there is a one-time lump-sum death payment. Later, you may be able to switch between the survivor benefit and your own; compare which pays more and when.
props: Report the death to SSA; funeral homes often do
Switching between own and survivor benefit later is worth comparing
Age 50 if disabled; any age while caring for the deceased's child who is under 16 or disabled and entitled to child's benefits
Children receive benefits under 18 (19 if a secondary-school student)
There is a one-time lump-sum death payment
The any-age benefit requires that the surviving spouse has not remarried

le:death-of-spouse:claims.plain: Life insurance and retirement accounts pay the named beneficiary directly. A surviving spouse who inherits an IRA can treat it as their own, roll it over, or keep it as an inherited IRA. The choice matters if the surviving spouse is under 59½.
props: Life insurance and retirement accounts pay the named beneficiary directly
A spouse can treat an inherited IRA as own, roll it over, or keep it inherited

le:death-of-spouse:taxes.plain: You can still file a joint return for the year your spouse died. After that, if you have a dependent child, you can file as a qualifying surviving spouse for two more years. Otherwise you file as single — often with about the same income but narrower tax brackets. Inherited assets usually get a stepped-up cost basis, and in community-property states both halves of shared property can.
props: Joint filing allowed for the year of death
QSS status for two more years with a dependent child
Otherwise single, often similar income with narrower brackets
Inherited assets generally get a stepped-up basis; community property both halves

le:death-of-spouse:update.plain: Your own will, powers of attorney and beneficiary forms probably name your spouse. Replace them, and take the diagnostic again as a one-person household.
props: Own documents probably name the spouse
Re-run the diagnostic for one person

pr:emergency-fund.plain: The usual target is three to six months of essential costs — not of income — kept in an insured account you can reach quickly. Start with a small fund of $1,000 or one month of costs, so a small surprise doesn't become new debt. Then build to the full target after getting your employer match and paying off high-interest debt. Aim higher, or beyond the range, if your income goes up and down, if one person supports the household, if you have dependents, or if finding a new job in your field takes a long time.
props: Target 3–6 months of essential expenses, not income
Held in an insured, liquid account
Starter fund of $1,000 or one month first
Full target after match and high-interest debt
Size higher for variable income, single earner, dependents, slow re-employment

pr:health.plain: Health coverage is a Tier-1 (top-priority) step for a reason: one hospital stay without insurance can turn a steady budget into debt you can't pay. ACA-compliant plans limit what you pay in-network each year (2026 limit: {{fig:aca_oop_max_self}} for one person, {{fig:aca_oop_max_family}} for a family). That limit, not the premium, is the amount your savings should aim to cover. If that is out of reach, check whether you qualify for Medicaid (the rules differ by state) or for cost-sharing reductions, which lower the limit on a Marketplace silver plan. Nonprofit hospitals must have a written financial assistance policy. Ask for it before you pay a large bill.
props: Health coverage is Tier-1 for a reason
One uninsured hospital stay can turn a stable budget into unpayable debt
ACA plans cap annual in-network out-of-pocket
Reserves should aim to cover that cap, not the premium
The cap has a one-person amount and a family amount
If the cap is out of reach, check Medicaid; its rules vary by state
Cost-sharing reductions lower the cap on a Marketplace silver plan
Nonprofit hospitals must have a written financial assistance policy
Ask for it before paying a large bill
before you pay a large bill

pr:disability.plain: For someone who works, becoming disabled is more likely than dying early, and your future pay is usually your biggest asset. Group long-term disability insurance often replaces about 60% of base pay. If your employer pays the premium, the benefit is taxed, so you really get less. The policy details that decide whether a claim pays — whether "disabled" means unable to do your own job or any job, how long you wait before benefits start, how long benefits last — matter as much as the percentage.
props: Disability is more likely than early death for working adults
Future income is usually the largest asset
Group LTD commonly replaces ~60% of base salary
Employer-paid premium → taxable benefit → lower real replacement
Own-occ vs any-occ, elimination period, benefit period matter as much

pr:term-life.plain: Life insurance replaces income for people who rely on it. If no one depends on you, you rarely need it. A common rule of thumb for a main earner with dependents is 10–12 times yearly income; the DIME method (debt + income for the years needed + mortgage + education) gives a number for your household. Term insurance is the standard choice for this job. Whole-life policies bundle insurance with a savings part that earns little.
props: Life insurance replaces income for dependents
Without dependents it is rarely needed
Heuristic 10–12× income for a primary earner with dependents
Term is the default; whole life bundles a low-return savings part

pr:property.plain: A landlord's policy covers the building, not a renter's belongings or a renter's liability. Renters insurance covers both. Homeowners should insure for what it would cost to rebuild, not what the home would sell for, and should know that standard policies don't cover flood.
props: Landlord's policy does not cover tenant property or liability
Insure to rebuild cost, not market value

pr:auto.plain: The minimum liability coverage states require is low, and it can leave your savings at risk after a bad accident. Consumer guides often suggest at least $100,000 per person, $300,000 per accident and $100,000 for property damage. Umbrella insurers usually require higher limits underneath before they will sell you a policy.
props: State minimum liability limits are low and can expose savings
Umbrella carriers require higher underlying limits

pr:umbrella.plain: An umbrella policy adds liability coverage on top of your auto and home policies. It costs little for the coverage you get — industry price surveys put $1 million at roughly $200–400 a year — and people often buy at least as much as their net worth.
props: Umbrella adds liability on top of auto and homeowners
on top of your auto and home
Commonly sized to at least net worth
at least as much as their net worth

pr:estate.plain: Beneficiary forms on retirement accounts and life insurance send that money straight to the people named, and they usually win over a will — so check them first. A will covers everything else, and it is where parents name a guardian for young children; without one, your state's law decides who gets what. A durable financial power of attorney lets a person you choose handle your money if you can't; without one, your family may need a court to appoint someone. A healthcare directive (a living will plus a healthcare proxy) records the care you want and who decides for you, and a HIPAA authorization lets people you name get your medical information. State law governs each of these.
props: Beneficiary designations pass assets directly and generally override a will; check first
A will directs everything else and names a guardian for minors
Without a will, state intestacy law decides
Durable POA lets a chosen person manage finances on incapacity
Without one, a court-appointed guardian/conservator may be needed
Healthcare directive = living will + proxy: wishes and decision-maker
living will plus a healthcare proxy
A HIPAA authorization lets named people get medical information
Each is governed by state law

pr:identity.plain: A security freeze stops anyone from opening new credit in your name. It's free by federal law at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, it doesn't change your credit score, and you can lift it for a while when you apply for credit. You can check your own credit reports for free every week at AnnualCreditReport.com. If fraud happens, IdentityTheft.gov makes a recovery plan for you, and telling your bank quickly about electronic transfers you didn't make limits how much you can lose.
props: A freeze stops new credit in your name
stops anyone from opening new credit
Free by federal law at all three bureaus
Can be lifted temporarily to apply
Prompt reporting of unauthorized electronic transfers limits liability

ar:limits.plain: Contribution limits change every January. For 2026: 401(k)/403(b) employee deferral {{fig:limit_401k_deferral}} (extra catch-up at 50+ {{fig:limit_401k_catchup_50}}; ages 60–63 {{fig:limit_401k_supercatchup_6063}}), IRA {{fig:limit_ira}} (catch-up {{fig:limit_ira_catchup}}), HSA {{fig:limit_hsa_self}} self-only / {{fig:limit_hsa_family}} family. Raise your payroll elections so the money goes in evenly through the year. You choose your health FSA ({{fig:limit_health_fsa}}) and dependent-care FSA ({{fig:limit_dcfsa}}) amounts at open enrollment.
props: 2026 limits for 401(k), catch-ups, IRA, HSA (figures layer)
Raise payroll elections to spread the deferral across the year
FSA elections are made at open enrollment

ar:credit.plain: Look at all three credit reports at AnnualCreditReport.com for accounts you don't recognize, and make sure a security freeze is on at each bureau.
props: Check all three reports for unrecognized accounts
Confirm a freeze at each bureau
freeze is on at each bureau

ar:withholding.plain: File last year's tax return by the April deadline. You can still put money into an IRA or HSA for last year until that deadline. An extension does not give you more time for this. Then use the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator with a recent pay stub. File a new W-4 if it shows you'll owe or get back a lot — especially after a raise, a second job, a marriage or a new child. If you pay estimated tax, mark the four due dates on your calendar: April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15.
props: File last year's return by the April deadline
A prior-year IRA or HSA contribution can be made until the filing deadline
ira or hsa for last year
Extensions do not extend that contribution deadline
extension does not give you more time
Run the estimator after filing, with a current pay stub
File a new W-4 if the projection is far from zero
Especially after raise, second job, marriage, new child
Estimated-tax payers: the four due dates April 15, June 15, September 15, January 15

ar:net-worth.plain: Add up what you own and subtract what you owe, on the same date each year. The change from year to year is the only number that shows real progress. The list itself is what your family would need in an emergency.
props: Net worth = assets minus liabilities, same date each year
Year-over-year change is the only real progress measure
only number that shows real progress
The list doubles as the family's emergency inventory

ar:subscriptions.plain: Look through a few months of statements for charges that repeat. Bank fees — overdraft, ATM, monthly service fees — often cost more than any one subscription and deserve the same look.
props: Bank fees often cost more than any single subscription

ar:rebalance.plain: Compare your current mix of investments to your target. If any part has drifted outside its allowed range, rebalance. Buying and selling inside an IRA or 401(k) is not taxed, so make the changes there first. In taxable accounts, put new contributions into whatever is short, so you don't have to sell at a gain.
props: Trades inside an IRA or 401(k) are not taxed, so rebalance there first
In taxable accounts, steer new contributions to avoid realizing gains
put new contributions into whatever is short

ar:insurance.plain: Most employers hold open enrollment in the fall. Check your health plan choice, your disability coverage, your term life against who depends on you and what you owe, and whether your home, auto and umbrella liability limits still fit your net worth. If you have Medicare, compare Part D and Medicare Advantage plans during open enrollment, October 15 to December 7. Costs, benefits and providers can change each year.
props: Open enrollment is usually in the fall
Term life vs current dependents and debts
On Medicare: compare Part D and Medicare Advantage plans October 15 to December 7
Medicare plan costs, benefits and providers can change each year

ar:beneficiaries.plain: Open every retirement account, life insurance policy and transfer-on-death registration and check who is named. Make sure your will, power of attorney and healthcare directive still name the right people.
props: Confirm beneficiaries on every account, policy, TOD registration
Check will, POA and directive still name the right people

ar:year-end.plain: Before December 31: sell investments at a loss in taxable accounts if it helps, take any required minimum distribution, make planned gifts to charity or qualified charitable distributions, and use the yearly gift exclusion ({{fig:gift_annual_exclusion}} per person for 2026) if you're giving to anyone.
props: Use the annual gift exclusion if gifting
